[strategy/guidance/technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-001-ai-automation-classification-guidance.md#purpose-statement]

### Purpose Statement

This guidance defines the four-tier enterprise AI and automation taxonomy and provides practitioners with the decision framework to classify any AI or automation capability correctly before scoping, building, or governing it. Misclassification leads to either under-governance (applying no AI governance to an LLM-based reasoning system) or over-governance (applying software engineering quality gates to a deterministic trigger-based workflow).
page_texts.5:
[strategy/guidance/technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-001-ai-automation-classification-guidance.md#business-value]

### Business Value

Correct classification routes build requests to the right role tier, sets the appropriate governance posture, and prevents the accumulation of AI governance debt that arises when capability types are conflated. It also provides the vocabulary required for the capability registry and intake process.
page_texts.6:
[strategy/guidance/technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-001-ai-automation-classification-guidance.md#target-audience]

### Target Audience

- **Primary Audience**: Enterprise architects, solution architects, and platform governance team members performing intake review
- **Secondary Audience**: High-Tech practitioners (Arch, Dev, Infra) evaluating capability requests from Mid-Tech and Low-Tech roles
- **Stakeholders**: Domain Product Owners proposing new AI or automation capabilities
page_texts.8:
[strategy/guidance/technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-001-ai-automation-classification-guidance.md#applicable-scenarios]

#### Applicable Scenarios

- A team is proposing a new automation or AI capability and needs to classify it before scoping
- An architect is evaluating which approach to recommend for a given use case
- Governance or compliance stakeholders need to understand what type of capability is being operated
- An existing capability is evolving (e.g., an RPA bot gaining AI-driven decision logic) and requires reclassification
page_texts.9:
[strategy/guidance/technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-001-ai-automation-classification-guidance.md#scope-boundaries]

#### Scope Boundaries

- **In Scope**: Classification of any software capability that automates tasks, processes data, or reasons about goals using AI
- **Out of Scope**: Selection of a specific vendor tool within a category — tool selection within each category is governed by enterprise standards and platform licensing decisions
- **Related Guidance**: [GUID-TEC-AI-002: Enterprise Agent Governance Guidance](./GUID-TEC-AI-002-enterprise-agent-governance-guidance.md) covers how to govern AI Agents and Custom AI Agents once classified

[strategy/guidance/technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-001-ai-automation-classification-guidance.md#business-drivers]

#### Business Drivers

- AI and automation capabilities are being created across delivery, PMO, and engineering functions using platforms with widely varying capability profiles and governance requirements
- Without a shared classification vocabulary, teams apply inconsistent governance expectations to capabilities that carry materially different risk profiles
- The enterprise AI governance framework (ADR-GOV-011) requires that all capabilities be classified before intake review proceeds

[strategy/guidance/technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-001-ai-automation-classification-guidance.md#strategic-alignment]

#### Strategic Alignment

This guidance is the classification layer of the enterprise AI governance strategy. It is the entry point for any new capability proposal and is a prerequisite for the capability registry intake process.

[strategy/guidance/technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-001-ai-automation-classification-guidance.md#current-state-assessment]

#### Current State Assessment

- M365 Copilot, Copilot Studio, Power Automate, and custom AI development (LLM APIs, orchestration frameworks) are all in active use across delivery teams
- The same platform (e.g., Copilot Studio) can be used to build both deterministic workflow automation and LLM-reasoning AI agents, creating classification ambiguity when teams classify by platform rather than behavior

[strategy/guidance/technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-001-ai-automation-classification-guidance.md#future-state-vision]

#### Future State Vision

- All capability proposals include a mandatory taxonomy classification that is reviewed during intake
- Capabilities that evolve across category boundaries are reclassified and brought under the appropriate governance posture
page_texts.18:
[strategy/guidance/technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-001-ai-automation-classification-guidance.md#problem-description]

#### Problem Description

When practitioners classify a capability as "AI" because it was built on an AI platform — regardless of whether it involves LLM reasoning — the organization applies AI governance overhead to deterministic workflows that do not require it, and simultaneously fails to apply AI governance to LLM-based systems that do. Both misclassifications degrade the value of the governance framework.

page_texts.21:
[strategy/guidance/technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-001-ai-automation-classification-guidance.md#principle-1-classify-by-behavior-not-by-platform]

#### Principle 1: Classify by Behavior, Not by Platform

**Description:** A capability's classification is determined by whether it reasons about what to do or executes what it was told to do — not by the platform it was built on.

**Rationale:** The same platform can host both deterministic workflows and LLM-reasoning agents. Classification by platform collapses the governance posture to the platform's highest-risk capability, which is incorrect for deterministic components.

**Application:** When evaluating a capability, ask: does the system need an LLM to interpret intent at runtime, or can the logic be fully authored in advance? If the logic can be fully authored, the capability is Automation regardless of what platform hosts it.
page_texts.22:
[strategy/guidance/technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-001-ai-automation-classification-guidance.md#principle-2-apply-independent-governance-to-each-layer]

#### Principle 2: Apply Independent Governance to Each Layer

**Description:** When a platform capability combines an LLM reasoning layer with a deterministic workflow layer, classify and govern each layer independently.

**Rationale:** An AI agent that invokes a pre-authored workflow as a tool action contains two distinct governance concerns: the LLM reasoning layer (AI Agent governance applies) and the workflow it invokes (Automation governance applies). The presence of an LLM elsewhere in the platform does not change the classification of the workflow layer.

**Application:** For composite capabilities, document each layer separately in the capability contract and apply the governance requirements of each layer independently.
page_texts.23:
[strategy/guidance/technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-001-ai-automation-classification-guidance.md#principle-3-escalate-rather-than-extend]

#### Principle 3: Escalate Rather Than Extend

**Description:** When a capability reaches the boundary of its category — for example, a configured AI agent that requires integration depth beyond platform connectors — escalate to the appropriate category rather than extending the capability beyond its design intent.

**Rationale:** Extending capabilities beyond their category boundary creates brittle implementations with undocumented governance exposure. A configured agent extended with custom code to bypass platform limitations should be reclassified as a Custom AI Agent with full engineering quality gates.

**Application:** Use the escalation path defined in this guidance when a capability reaches a category boundary.
page_texts.25:
[strategy/guidance/technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-001-ai-automation-classification-guidance.md#approach-1-the-four-tier-taxonomy]

#### Approach 1: The Four-Tier Taxonomy

**Overview:** All enterprise AI and automation capabilities classify into one of four categories based on reasoning behavior and integration pattern.

**When to Use:** Apply this taxonomy to every new capability proposal and every existing capability that is evolving in scope.

**Implementation:**

| Category | Definition | Reasoning | Integration Point |
|---|---|---|---|
| Automation (RPA and Workflow) | Deterministic, rule-authored, executes predefined steps without judgment | None | UI layer (RPA) or API/connector layer (Workflow) |
| Intelligent Automation | RPA extended with AI-powered perception (OCR, document intelligence, NL classification) to handle unstructured inputs; execution remains deterministic | Perception only (no goal-directed reasoning) | UI + AI extraction layer |
| AI Agents (Configured) | LLM acts as reasoning engine; interprets goal or intent at runtime and decides steps; built through declarative configuration without custom code | Goal-directed LLM reasoning | Platform connectors |
| Custom AI Agents | LLM-driven systems built through custom software development; full control over reasoning logic, tool integration, and output handling | Full agentic reasoning | Any API or system |

**Considerations:** Some platforms market deterministic workflow features as "AI-powered." Evaluate the actual reasoning behavior, not the marketing classification.
page_texts.26:
[strategy/guidance/technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-001-ai-automation-classification-guidance.md#approach-2-the-classification-decision-table]

#### Approach 2: The Classification Decision Table

**Overview:** A structured decision table for routing any capability proposal to the correct category.

**When to Use:** During intake review, when a capability proposal does not clearly map to a single category.

| If the use case is... | Classify as... |
|---|---|
| Repetitive, structured, UI-based data movement with no judgment required | Automation — RPA |
| Event-triggered API orchestration with fixed steps and connectors | Automation — Workflow |
| Processing unstructured inputs (PDFs, emails, images) before executing fixed steps | Intelligent Automation |
| Answering natural language questions using connected knowledge or data | AI Agents (Configured) |
| Completing goals where the steps cannot be fully specified in advance | AI Agents (Configured) |
| Deep system integration, custom reasoning logic, or requirements beyond platform connectors | Custom AI Agents |
| High-volume automation with strict SLA requirements and zero tolerance for non-determinism | Automation (RPA or Workflow) |
| Compliance, audit, or security requirements that exceed platform governance capabilities | Custom AI Agents |
page_texts.28:
[strategy/guidance/technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-001-ai-automation-classification-guidance.md#best-practice-1-classify-before-scoping]

#### Best Practice 1: Classify Before Scoping

**Description:** Require taxonomy classification as the first step in any capability intake, before scoping, tooling selection, or build assignment.

**Rationale:** Classification determines governance posture, build tier, and tooling scope. Scoping a capability before classifying it leads to wasted effort when the wrong build tier is assigned or the wrong platform is selected.

**Implementation:** The capability intake form must include a taxonomy classification field with the four categories and require the proposer to select one with a brief rationale.

**Success Indicators:** All capabilities in the capability registry have a taxonomy classification recorded at intake.
page_texts.29:
[strategy/guidance/technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-001-ai-automation-classification-guidance.md#best-practice-2-reclassify-on-evolution]

#### Best Practice 2: Reclassify on Evolution

**Description:** Review capabilities for reclassification whenever their scope, integration depth, or reasoning behavior changes materially.

**Rationale:** A capability that begins as Intelligent Automation and gains conversational reasoning capabilities has crossed into the AI Agents category and must be brought under AI agent governance.

**Implementation:** Include a taxonomy classification review in the quarterly capability boundary review cadence.

**Success Indicators:** No capabilities with LLM reasoning layers are classified as Automation; no capabilities with added custom code are classified as AI Agents (Configured).
page_texts.31:
[strategy/guidance/technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-001-ai-automation-classification-guidance.md#pitfall-1-classifying-by-platform-name]

#### Pitfall 1: Classifying by Platform Name

**Description:** Calling a capability "an AI agent" because it was built in a platform whose name includes "AI" or "Copilot," regardless of whether it involves LLM reasoning.

**Impact:** Applies AI governance overhead to deterministic workflows unnecessarily; creates inaccurate portfolio reporting.

**Prevention:** Always ask the primary classification question: does this system reason about what to do, or execute what it was told to do?

**Mitigation:** During intake review, require the proposer to describe the capability's decision logic in plain language. If the description is a fixed sequence of steps, it is Automation.
page_texts.32:
[strategy/guidance/technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-001-ai-automation-classification-guidance.md#pitfall-2-treating-category-as-permanent]

#### Pitfall 2: Treating Category as Permanent

**Description:** Classifying a capability once and never revisiting the classification as the capability evolves.

**Impact:** Capabilities that have gained LLM reasoning or custom code operate under an incorrect governance posture, accumulating compliance exposure.

**Prevention:** Include taxonomy reclassification as a standing agenda item in quarterly boundary reviews.

**Mitigation:** Require a classification review for any capability undergoing a scope change, new integration, or platform migration.
page_texts.33:
[strategy/guidance/technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-001-ai-automation-classification-guidance.md#pitfall-3-using-custom-ai-agent-when-configured-agent-is-sufficient]

#### Pitfall 3: Using Custom AI Agent When Configured Agent Is Sufficient

**Description:** Engineering teams default to custom code for AI agent builds even when a configured agent platform can meet the requirements.

**Impact:** Custom code carries engineering overhead, long-term maintenance cost, and full engineering quality gate requirements. Using it unnecessarily increases delivery time and governance burden.

**Prevention:** Apply the escalation path: start with configured AI agent platforms and escalate to Custom AI Agent only when a specific integration, quality, or control requirement cannot be met in-platform.

[strategy/guidance/technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-001-ai-automation-classification-guidance.md#preparation-steps]

#### Preparation Steps

1. **Add taxonomy classification to the capability intake form**

    - Required inputs: the four taxonomy categories with definitions
    - Key activity: the proposer selects the category that best describes the capability's reasoning behavior and provides a one-sentence rationale
    - Expected output: a recorded taxonomy classification for every intake proposal

2. **Train intake reviewers on the classification criteria**

    - Required inputs: this guidance document; the classification anti-patterns section
    - Key activity: reviewers should be able to challenge a proposed classification by applying the primary classification question and the decision table
    - Expected output: intake reviewers can identify and correct the three most common classification anti-patterns
page_texts.43:
[strategy/guidance/technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-001-ai-automation-classification-guidance.md#execution-steps]

#### Execution Steps

1. **Apply classification during intake review**

    - Review the proposer's classification against the decision table
    - If the capability combines multiple layers (e.g., an AI agent that invokes workflows), classify each layer independently and document both
    - Record the classification and rationale in the capability registry

2. **Assign governance posture based on classification**

    - Automation (RPA and Workflow): process automation governance; no AI governance required
    - Intelligent Automation: process automation governance plus AI model accuracy monitoring
    - AI Agents (Configured): full AI agent governance — STD-TEC-AI-001 through STD-TEC-AI-008 and STD-GOV-AI-004 through STD-GOV-AI-005 apply
    - Custom AI Agents: AI agent governance plus engineering quality gates (code review, automated testing, CI/CD, security review)
page_texts.44:
[strategy/guidance/technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-001-ai-automation-classification-guidance.md#validation-steps]

#### Validation Steps

1. **Validate classification accuracy during quarterly boundary review**
    - Review any capabilities that have changed scope, gained new integrations, or received behavior change reports since the last review
    - Reclassify as needed and update the capability registry
page_texts.46:
[strategy/guidance/technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-001-ai-automation-classification-guidance.md#decision-point-1-does-this-capability-involve-llm-reasoning]

#### Decision Point 1: Does This Capability Involve LLM Reasoning?

**Context:** The first classification question for any new or evolving capability.

**Options:** Yes (LLM interprets intent and decides steps at runtime) or No (logic is fully authored; system executes what it was told)

**Criteria:** Can the full process logic be authored in advance as a deterministic rule or sequence? If yes, the capability is Automation or Intelligent Automation. If no, it is an AI Agent.

**Recommendation:** When in doubt, describe what the system does when it receives an ambiguous or unexpected input. If the answer is "it executes the authored fallback rule," it is Automation. If the answer is "it reasons about the best response," it is an AI Agent.
page_texts.47:
[strategy/guidance/technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-001-ai-automation-classification-guidance.md#decision-point-2-does-the-capability-require-custom-code]

#### Decision Point 2: Does the Capability Require Custom Code?

**Context:** Distinguishing AI Agents (Configured) from Custom AI Agents.

**Options:** Configured (behavior defined through system prompts, knowledge sources, and tool definitions without custom code) or Custom (behavior implemented through custom software using LLM APIs and orchestration frameworks)

**Criteria:** Can all required integrations, output handling, and reasoning constraints be met within the platform's configuration model? If yes, use a Configured AI Agent. If no, escalate to Custom AI Agent.

**Recommendation:** Apply the escalation principle: start with the configured agent approach. Only escalate to Custom AI Agent when a specific requirement cannot be met in-platform.

page_texts.50:
[strategy/guidance/technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-001-ai-automation-classification-guidance.md#use-case-1-trigger-based-workflow-in-copilot-studio]

#### Use Case 1: Trigger-Based Workflow in Copilot Studio

**Scenario Description:** A PM team wants to use Copilot Studio to build a workflow that sends a notification and creates a task whenever a project record reaches a specific status.

**Context:** The capability is built in a platform that also supports AI agents. The workflow itself executes a fixed sequence of steps when triggered.

**Guidance Application:** Despite being built in Copilot Studio (an AI platform), this capability is Automation — Workflow. It executes an authored sequence with no LLM reasoning. It does not require AI agent governance standards. Process automation governance applies.

**Success Factors:** Classify based on behavior; document the classification and rationale in the capability registry.
page_texts.51:
[strategy/guidance/technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-001-ai-automation-classification-guidance.md#use-case-2-project-status-assistant-in-agent-builder]

#### Use Case 2: Project Status Assistant in Agent Builder

**Scenario Description:** A PM wants to build an agent in M365 Agent Builder that answers natural language questions about project status by reasoning across SharePoint and ADO data.

**Context:** The agent uses an LLM to interpret questions and decide which data to retrieve and how to synthesize an answer. The steps cannot be fully authored in advance.

**Guidance Application:** This is an AI Agent (Configured). It requires full AI agent governance: STD-TEC-AI-001 through STD-TEC-AI-008 and STD-GOV-AI-004 through STD-GOV-AI-005. The PM tier (Low-Tech) can build it, but a High-Tech governance review is required before Pilot-to-Production promotion.

**Success Factors:** Complete the capability contract and intent catalog before prompt authoring begins (see GUID-TEC-AI-002).
page_texts.52:
[strategy/guidance/technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-001-ai-automation-classification-guidance.md#use-case-3-document-intelligence-pipeline]

#### Use Case 3: Document Intelligence Pipeline

**Scenario Description:** A QA team wants to extract defect information from unstructured test reports (PDF) and route them to the correct defect queue based on extracted values.

**Context:** The capability uses AI-powered document intelligence to extract data from unstructured documents; the routing logic is deterministic.

**Guidance Application:** This is Intelligent Automation. The AI component handles perception (extracting structured data from unstructured inputs); the routing logic is authored and deterministic. Governance requires process automation governance plus AI model accuracy monitoring. Mid-Tech (QA) can lead the build with High-Tech support for model configuration.

page_texts.63:
[strategy/guidance/technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-001-ai-automation-classification-guidance.md#success-criteria]

### Success Criteria

The classification process is operating effectively when the following outcomes are achieved:

| Metric | Target | Measurement Method |
|---|---|---|
| % of capabilities correctly classified on first intake submission | High and stable | Intake review audit — compare initial classification to governance reviewer's determination |
| Reclassification rate after intake | Declining over time | Change log for classification decisions; root cause analysis for repeated reclassification patterns |
| % of practitioners who can correctly classify a sample capability without facilitation after completing onboarding | High and stable | Onboarding assessment; periodic spot-checks with representative classification scenarios |
| Time to complete classification during intake review | Declining over time as practitioners gain experience | Intake timestamp records |
page_texts.64:
[strategy/guidance/technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-001-ai-automation-classification-guidance.md#assessment-cadence]

### Assessment Cadence

- **Quarterly intake review**: The Platform Governance Team reviews classification accuracy and reclassification patterns from the prior quarter. Persistent misclassification patterns (e.g., Intelligent Automation routinely submitted as AI Agent) are addressed with clarification examples or taxonomy refinements.
- **Annual taxonomy review**: The Enterprise Copilot Architecture Board reviews the four-tier taxonomy for structural changes driven by platform evolution, new capability types, or persistent misclassification patterns.
